title: Expectations
hook: The same result can feel like a win or a failure depending on the line you drew first.
counterintuition: Expectations do not only predict how you will feel later. They shape the baseline you judge against, the effort others receive, and the disappointment you call evidence.
tryThisNow: Before judging one result today, write the baseline you expected, the result you got, and the result you would have judged fairly before the forecast feeling arrived.
keyTakeaway: Set the baseline before the result, or expectations will quietly rewrite what counts as good enough.

breakdown.fastRead:
The postmortem note on Harper's municipal court lunch calendar says the new meal slot failed because clerks looked disappointed. Last week, the court promised hot lunches every day. This week, two days were sandwiches. Harper marks expectations on the note and compares the change with the old baseline: skipped lunches and late dockets.

Expectations become a measuring line. Put the line too high, and a real gain can feel like failure. Put it too low, and a weak result can feel generous. The result has not changed. The reference point has.

Feelings need a baseline before they testify.
breakdown.deepRead:
Harper's postmortem note is not wrong about disappointment. People did expect hot food. The question is whether disappointment should cancel the lunch calendar or reveal a promise problem. Harper writes baseline on the note, then separates two judgments: did the new calendar improve docket coverage, and did the promise inflate what clerks thought they were getting?

Expectations work before the result arrives. A forecast creates a mental contract. If reality beats the contract, you feel pleased. If reality misses it, you feel cheated. This can help planning when the contract is clear and fair. It can distort judgment when the contract was vague, inflated, or planted by someone with something to sell. A ten-minute delay feels fine after a forty-minute warning and unbearable after a two-minute promise.

The baseline carries the emotion.

Elliot sees the same effect in a hospice donation letter. A commitment card says donors will “double comfort this winter,” and the campaign team expects a record return. The first mailing beats last year's response but misses the inflated target. Elliot marks baseline on the card and chooses a second test from last year's true rate, not from the emotional promise in the draft.

The correction is to write the reference line before the result works on you. What did you expect? Who set that expectation? What would you have called acceptable before the forecast feeling arrived? That question does not make you cold. It keeps disappointment from pretending to be measurement.
breakdown.fullRead:
The open-loop list on Bea's college add-drop desk is full of students waiting for a popular psychology seminar. The professor told advisers the new section would “solve the pressure.” It added twelve seats and left twenty students outside. Parents are angry. Bea marks placebo on the list because the promised relief may be shaping the pain more than the actual seat count. Before changing the deadline rule, she compares the new waitlist with the old one.

Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson's Pygmalion work showed how expectations can change treatment, not just judgment. When teachers expected certain students to bloom, those students could receive different attention, patience, and opportunities. The label did not merely sit in a notebook. It altered the field around the student.

That is the hard part: expectations can be both false and powerful.

You see the same force in markets. A company can earn strong profits and fall because investors expected even more. Another can lose money and rise because the loss was less bad than feared. The result is filtered through the baseline. The surprise, not the raw number, drives the first feeling.

Dina faces a smaller version in ceramics defect pricing. A news alert queue says a boutique kiln has “museum-grade consistency.” Three bowls arrive with tiny glaze freckles. Customers call the batch a disaster because the promise left no room for handmade variation. Dina marks disappointment on the queue and sets the refund policy against the stated grade and the normal defect rate, not against outrage alone.

Expectations can also heal or harm through the body. A placebo can reduce pain because the person expects relief. A nocebo can intensify symptoms because the person expects trouble. You do not have to fake certainty to use this knowledge. You have to be careful with promises. A forecast can become part of the experience it claims only to describe.

Cecilia learns that at a ferry terminal passenger sign. The clipboard from the information desk shows three versions of a delay notice: “five minutes,” “about twenty minutes,” and “boarding when visibility clears.” The five-minute promise creates anger every time fog lingers. Cecilia marks forecast feeling on the clipboard and chooses the message that prepares passengers without inventing precision.

Which expectation did you install before you judged the outcome?

Nicolette sees the postmortem version in a bakery noon-leftover test. A sealed envelope held the owner's forecast: the new almond rolls would sell out by noon. They sold better than the old rolls but left two trays at closing. The team called it failure. Nicolette marks expectations on the envelope and changes the next test standard to margin, waste, and repeat orders written before the bake.

Set the baseline before the result, or expectations will quietly rewrite what counts as good enough.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Expectations turn forecasts into judgment lines. Readers need to separate result quality from disappointment, inflated baselines, and promise effects.

reviewCards.front: A good result feels bad after a bigger promise. Which baseline should reset the judgment?
reviewCards.back: Compare the result with the original baseline and with the promised one. Disappointment may come from the inflated promise, not the actual outcome.

reviewCards.front: Why should baselines be written before results arrive?
reviewCards.back: Once the result arrives, forecast feeling rewrites what seems fair. A prewritten baseline protects the judgment from disappointment or relief.

reviewCards.front: How can expectations affect people instead of just ratings?
reviewCards.back: Expectations can change attention, patience, and opportunity. The Pygmalion pattern shows that a label can alter the treatment someone receives.

reviewCards.front: A delay notice keeps making passengers angry. What is the expectation check?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the message installed false precision. A fair forecast should prepare people without creating a promise the system cannot keep.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between disappointment and evidence?
reviewCards.back: Disappointment tells you a baseline was missed. Evidence tells you whether the result is good against a fair standard.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Treat expectations as part of the measurement system. Before you judge a result, identify who set the baseline and whether the baseline was fair.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a result feels disappointing, then I will compare it with the pre-result baseline before calling it failure.
If a message sets a forecast, then I will ask whether people can fairly judge the result against it later.
If a label raises or lowers expectations for a person, then I will check whether it changes the attention or opportunities they receive.
If customers are angry after a partial improvement, then I will separate product performance from the expectation created by the promise.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one result arrives, write the baseline you will use to judge it. Afterward, compare your reaction with that prewritten line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit one disappointment. Identify the original baseline, the promised baseline, and the fair baseline you would set now.
